title: Automated reduction of fault-tolerant circuits
authors: Hyeongjun Jeon, Jeonghoon Lee, Taehyun Kim
abstract: We present an automated method for reducing fault-tolerant circuits through fault-equivalent rewrites. Starting from a known fault-tolerant circuit, the search applies non-reducing enabling rules to expose Bell-pair reductions, each of which removes an ancilla preparation and a CNOT gate. Because every search transition preserves fault equivalence, the resulting circuits inherit the fault-tolerance properties of the input circuit. Candidate circuits are evaluated using circuit-level Monte Carlo simulation. For Shor-style syndrome extraction with the $[[7,1,3]]$ code, our method reduces one syndrome-measurement round from 30 to 18 ancilla preparations and from 54 to 42 CNOT gates. At a physical two-qubit error rate of $p = 10^{-3}$, the optimized circuit lowers the logical error rate by approximately 21% for both logical basis states. The reduction ranges from 13% to 23% over a range of $p$ spanning two orders of magnitude. We also apply the method to Steane-based dynamic syndrome extraction constructed from Goto's verified logical-$\lvert 0 \rangle$ preparation, in which the verification qubit serves as a flag. The search selects a circuit using four ancillas and 14 CNOT gates, matching the resource counts of the previous design but with an improved CNOT depth. Under depolarizing idle noise at $3p/10$ the selected circuit lowers the logical error rate by approximately 15% for both logical basis states, and by approximately $10%$ at $p/10$. These results demonstrate that automated fault-equivalent rewriting can identify circuits with lower resource costs or improved logical performance without separately verifying the fault tolerance of every candidate.
summary: This paper introduces an automated technique to simplify fault-tolerant quantum circuits by performing fault-equivalent rewrites. By systematically searching for reductions, the authors significantly decrease resource requirements (like CNOT gates) and improve the logical error rate for codes like the Steane code. This work provides a powerful, scalable tool for designing more efficient quantum hardware protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for an automated method to reduce the resource cost and improve the logical performance of fault-tolerant quantum circuits.
main_result: The automated rewriting method successfully reduced the required ancilla preparations and CNOT gates for syndrome extraction, leading to a demonstrated logical error rate reduction of up to 23% for the [[7, 1, 3]] code.
method: The core method is an automated search procedure utilizing fault-equivalent rewrites, which applies non-reducing enabling rules to expose Bell-pair reductions while preserving fault-tolerance.
model_or_system: The study focuses on fault-tolerant quantum computation, specifically optimizing syndrome-extraction gadgets for Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECCs) like the [[7, 1, 3]] Steane code.
key_observables: Logical error rate, number of ancilla preparations, number of CNOT gates, and circuit depth.
important_parameters: Physical two-qubit error rate ($p$), and noise models including dephasing and depolarizing idle noise.
main_assumptions: The search procedure assumes that the composite reduction matcher returns finitely many matches, and performance evaluation relies on computationally expensive Monte Carlo simulations.
figures_summary: Figures compare logical error rates versus physical error rate ($p$) or number of cycles ($N$) for various syndrome-extraction protocols, showing performance improvements for the optimized circuits.
paper_structure: The paper details the automated search framework using fault-equivalent rewrites, applies this to specific QEC codes (Shor/Steane), and evaluates the resulting circuits by comparing resource counts and simulating logical error rates under various noise models.
why_interesting: The development of automated, systematic tools for circuit optimization is crucial for scaling quantum computation, providing concrete blueprints for hardware implementation.
